title: Grab and Move + WSLg windows
author: awilkins
summary: Grab and Move relocates WSLg window pixels without keeping the Linux surface's pointer coordinate mapping synchronized; moving the same window through the native title bar restores alignment.
next_action: Approve a focused compatibility design and reproduce the move on a scaled WSLg desktop.

confidence.rationale: The symptom and native-move recovery strongly identify the move lifecycle, but the exact WSLg notification or coordinate boundary still needs a focused reproduction.

judgment.rationale: Two independent reports show that Grab and Move visually relocates WSLg windows while their Linux-side input hit-testing remains at an offset proportional to the drag. Native taskbar movement repairs the mapping, which points to the synthetic move path rather than the WSLg application.
evidence: The original report reproduces horizontal and vertical click offsets after moving an Eclipse WSLg window.
A second reporter reproduces the same offset in Nautilus and notes that native taskbar movement restores correct pointer mapping.
The second report observes a larger mismatch around 200% display scale, making DPI/coordinate conversion a useful discriminator.
judgment.recommended_action: Approve a focused compatibility design and reproduce the move on a scaled WSLg desktop.

fix_assessment.rationale: No existing fix attempt covers the scoped PowerToys-owned path identified by this lightweight judgment.

proposed_fixes.title: Preserve WSLg input-coordinate synchronization during synthetic moves
proposed_fixes.root_cause: Grab and Move likely repositions WSLg top-level windows through a path that updates the visible host window without triggering the native move lifecycle used to refresh WSLg input coordinate mapping.
plan: Identify WSLg-hosted top-level windows and compare Grab and Move's positioning calls with a normal title-bar move.
Route compatible WSLg windows through a system move sequence or emit the required position/DPI notifications after movement.
If reliable synchronization is impossible, prevent Grab and Move from handling WSLg windows and explain the limitation.
verification: Move Eclipse and Nautilus WSLg windows horizontally and vertically at 100% and 200% scaling and verify click targets remain aligned.
Verify native Win32/UWP window movement and multi-monitor dragging remain unchanged.

confidence.rationale: The symptom and native-move recovery strongly identify the move lifecycle, but the exact WSLg notification or coordinate boundary still needs a focused reproduction.

issue_context.summary: Grab and Move relocates WSLg window pixels without keeping the Linux surface's pointer coordinate mapping synchronized; moving the same window through the native title bar restores alignment.
known_information: The problem affects at least Eclipse and Nautilus WSLg windows.
The pointer offset grows with the drag vector and occurs on both axes.
A normal title-bar move or minimize/restore can restore correct hit testing.
inferences: Grab and Move's synthetic positioning path may bypass a move lifecycle or coordinate update that WSLg's remoting surface relies on.
DPI scaling may amplify the stale coordinate transform but is not yet proven to be the sole cause.
issue_context.analysis: The repeatable geometric offset and recovery through native window movement make this suitable for a bounded compatibility design. The safest design should compare native move semantics with the current Grab and Move positioning path and either use a compatible move sequence or explicitly exclude unsupported WSLg surfaces.
initial_investigation: Reviewed the complete live body, both attached screenshots, the confirming Nautilus report, current labels, assignees, and timeline.
Found no linked upstream fix or active owner for this issue.

actions.label: Reproduce WSLg pointer-offset path
actions.note: Maintainer-side verification only; this artifact does not execute the steps or write upstream.

reproduce.version_requirement: Latest stable or Preview PowerToys build
prerequisites: A Linux GUI app such as Nautilus or Eclipse
One display at 100% and, if available, one at 200% scaling
steps: Open a WSLg app and click a known target.
Use Grab and Move to translate the window horizontally and vertically.
Click the same visible target and record the hit offset.
Move the window through its native title bar or minimize/restore, then retest.
reproduce.expected_result: The maintainer can determine whether the offset is introduced only by Grab and Move and whether native movement refreshes the WSLg input transform.
